content:
We can be certain that Apple will raise prices when it unveils the iPhone 18 Pro next month. Earlier, Apple raised prices across the board due to higher memory costs, but it did not simultaneously raise the prices of existing iPhone models at that time — but that was only a temporary respite.

However, two sources now indicate that the starting price for this year's Pro models will be $1,399 — even I find it hard to believe Apple would really go that far...

Don't get me wrong: Apple has made it very clear it wants to protect its profit margins and has never been afraid of big price hikes. For example, the base-model MacBook Air went from $1,099 to $1,299, a $200 increase. Even the MacBook Neo, which initially surprised people with its $599 starting price, has already gone up by $100.

But a $300 increase to the iPhone Pro starting price is simply outrageous. That kind of jump has historically only been applied to products with much higher price tags.

Among products that have received $300 price hikes, the cheapest is the base-model MacBook Pro, which went from $1,699 to $1,999. That increase is indeed significant, nearly 18%. But a $300 increase for the iPhone 18 Pro over its predecessor works out to a 27% price hike.

The most upvoted comment comes from IndomitableSlake

Apple will charge whatever it wants, and customers will keep paying. The housing, automotive, and home appliance industries have already proven this. Why would this be any different? People will just take out loans. 120 years of social and economic history have proven that long-term debt brings absolutely no consequences; let's take out another loan.

Again, this price increase isn't entirely impossible. For example, the price of some MacBook configuration upgrades really did double; Apple does love making money. But Tim Cook did hint on an earnings call that the company wouldn't go to any lengths to protect profit margins.

As for sales, I do feel this price hike will put a lot of people off upgrading, especially given that next year's Pro models look set to be a bigger upgrade.

Of course, the counterargument is that the Apple Upgrade Program can ease some of the pressure. Some people might feel fine with leasing an iPhone 18 Pro for a year and upgrading to the 20th anniversary edition next year. But for those who buy outright, a price hike of this magnitude will be a major deterrent.

What do you think? Do you feel a $300 increase is reasonable, or is a 27% hike too much for Apple? Share your thoughts in the comments section.
